title: The Bridge of Paper Cranes
level_note: Original Fountas & Pinnell Guided Reading Level L practice material; not an official benchmark assessment.
passage:
Every spring, the children at Maple Street School made something for the neighborhood art walk. This year, their teacher, Mr. Ruiz, suggested a bridge of paper cranes. Each student would fold one bird and write a kind message on its wings. The class planned to hang the cranes between two tall posts outside the community center.

Nora chose yellow paper because it reminded her of sunshine. She wrote, “You can begin again tomorrow.” Then she folded one corner too far. The paper would not meet in the middle, and the crane leaned to one side. Nora crumpled the sheet and reached for another. Across the table, Ben was carefully flattening each crease with his thumbnail. His first crane stood straight, but he had written nothing on it.

“Would you show me how you make the wings even?” Nora asked. Ben turned his bird around and pointed to the folded edges. “I line up the corners first. Then I press the crease.” Nora tried again. This time the wings matched. “I like your message,” Ben said when he read it. He took a blue square and began writing. His words were, “Someone is glad you are here.”

The next afternoon, the class carried a basket of cranes to the community center. Mr. Ruiz tied each bird to a long cord. As the children worked, they noticed one space between the posts was wider than the others. The cord sagged there. Nora suggested moving two cranes closer together, but the cord still drooped. Ben found an empty wooden hoop in the center's craft room. The children fixed it under the cord and looped the middle around the hoop. Now the bridge held firm.

On the day of the art walk, people stopped beneath the bright paper bridge. A woman read Ben's message twice, then smiled at the children. Nora looked at her own crane. Its wings were not perfect, but her message was easy to read. She felt proud that she had kept trying—and glad that Ben had shared his idea.

questions.question_text: What did the class plan to make for the art walk?
choices: A bridge made of paper cranes
A row of painted wooden signs
A basket filled with real birds
A large map of the neighborhood
questions.correct_answer: A bridge made of paper cranes
questions.explanation: Mr. Ruiz suggests a bridge of paper cranes, and the class plans to hang them outside the community center.

questions.question_text: What were students asked to write on their paper cranes?
choices: A kind message
Their home address
A list of art supplies
The name of a bird
questions.explanation: The first paragraph says each student would write a kind message on the crane's wings.

questions.question_text: Why did Nora choose yellow paper?
choices: It reminded her of sunshine.
It was the only paper left.
Ben asked her to use it.
The community center was painted yellow.
questions.explanation: The story directly tells us that the yellow paper reminded Nora of sunshine.

questions.question_text: Why did Nora's first crane lean to one side?
choices: One corner was folded too far.
The yellow paper was too heavy.
Ben pulled one wing off.
The table was shaking.
questions.correct_answer: One corner was folded too far.
questions.explanation: Nora folds one corner too far, so the paper edges do not meet in the middle.

questions.question_text: What might Ben have been unsure about when Nora first saw him?
choices: What message to write on his crane
Where the community center was
How to fold a paper square
Which color the posts should be
questions.correct_answer: What message to write on his crane
questions.explanation: Ben has folded a crane but written nothing on it yet, so he may still be thinking of a message.

questions.question_text: What did Ben tell Nora to do before pressing the crease?
choices: Line up the corners
Write the message
Turn the paper blue
Cut off the folded edge
questions.explanation: Ben explains the steps: first line up the corners, then press the crease.

questions.question_text: In the story, what is a crease?
choices: A line made by folding paper
A spot of paint on a bird
A message written in blue ink
A string used to hang the cranes
questions.correct_answer: A line made by folding paper
questions.explanation: Ben presses the crease after lining up the corners, so a crease is the line left by a fold.

choices: Someone is glad you are here.
You can begin again tomorrow.
Look beneath the wooden hoop.
Welcome to Maple Street School.
questions.correct_answer: Someone is glad you are here.
questions.explanation: Ben writes, “Someone is glad you are here,” after reading Nora's message.

questions.question_text: Why did the cord sag between the posts?
choices: The space between the posts was wider there.
The cranes were made from wet paper.
Mr. Ruiz tied the birds to the basket.
The children forgot to bring the cord.
questions.correct_answer: The space between the posts was wider there.
questions.explanation: The children notice that one space is wider than the others, and the cord sags in that spot.

questions.question_text: What helped the paper-crane bridge hold firm?
choices: The children fixed a wooden hoop under the cord.
Nora tied every crane to the basket.
Ben added more paper to the widest space.
Mr. Ruiz moved the two tall posts together.
questions.correct_answer: The children fixed a wooden hoop under the cord.
questions.explanation: They loop the middle of the cord around an empty wooden hoop, which supports the sagging section.

questions.question_text: What does “the cord sagged” mean in this story?
choices: The cord drooped in the middle.
The cord snapped into pieces.
The cord changed to a different color.
The cord became longer by itself.
questions.correct_answer: The cord drooped in the middle.
questions.explanation: The next sentence says the cord drooped, and the children fix it by supporting the middle.

questions.question_text: Why might the woman have smiled after reading Ben's message?
choices: The kind words may have made her feel welcome.
She wanted to take the cranes home.
She was glad the art walk was over.
She had written the message herself.
questions.correct_answer: The kind words may have made her feel welcome.
questions.explanation: The message tells someone they are glad to have them there, and the woman smiles after reading it.

questions.question_text: How does Nora feel about her crane at the end?
choices: Proud that she kept trying, even though its wings were not perfect
Angry that Ben wrote a better message
Worried that the art walk will never begin
Disappointed that the crane is not made of wood
questions.correct_answer: Proud that she kept trying, even though its wings were not perfect
questions.explanation: Nora notices the wings are imperfect but feels proud that she continued and finished her message.

questions.question_text: Which idea is best supported by the story?
choices: Sharing what you know can help everyone make something together.
A project works best when one person does all the work.
Paper crafts should always look exactly alike.
Kind messages are only useful at school.
questions.correct_answer: Sharing what you know can help everyone make something together.
questions.explanation: Ben shares his folding method, Nora keeps practicing, and the children work together to support the bridge.

questions.question_text: Which sentence best summarizes the story?
choices: Nora and Ben help make a paper-crane display by sharing ideas and solving a problem together.
Nora visits the community center to learn how to grow flowers.
Ben folds a paper bird and hides it under the art table.
Mr. Ruiz asks the class to build two new posts for the center.
questions.correct_answer: Nora and Ben help make a paper-crane display by sharing ideas and solving a problem together.
questions.explanation: The story follows Nora and Ben as they learn from one another and solve the display's sagging-cord problem.
